artists.name: Scott Joplin
artists.summary: The leading composer of ragtime, whose syncopated piano pieces laid rhythmic groundwork that early jazz built on.
know: His Maple Leaf Rag sold widely as sheet music and made him the best known ragtime writer.
He wrote a full opera, Treemonisha, which was not properly staged until decades after his death.
The 1973 film The Sting used his rags and set off a big revival of his music.

cousins.why: A founding figure whose early form became the base for a whole tradition.
An early pioneer who set the template for the genre that followed.

artists.name: Jelly Roll Morton
artists.summary: An early New Orleans pianist and arranger who showed that jazz could be composed and arranged, not just improvised.
know: He loudly claimed to have invented jazz, a boast that overshadowed his real achievements.
His Red Hot Peppers recordings for Victor in the 1920s are models of tightly arranged small band jazz.
In 1938 he recorded long spoken and played interviews for the Library of Congress with Alan Lomax.

influencedBy.why: Learned ragtime from Joplin's pieces and demonstrated for Lomax how he loosened them into a jazz feel.

cousins.why: A self-mythologizing early figure whose legend grew alongside his music.
A colorful early showman who helped define a regional style.

artists.name: Ma Rainey
artists.summary: One of the first professional blues singers and among the first to record, she carried the blues from tent shows onto records. Her earthy, commanding style set the template for the classic blues era.
know: She was widely billed as the Mother of the Blues.
She recorded roughly 100 sides for Paramount between 1923 and 1928.
She toured with the Rabbit Foot Minstrels, where she crossed paths with a young Bessie Smith.
keyAlbums: Prove It on Me Blues (Paramount single)

cousins.why: Founding recording act that set the mold for a whole genre in the 1920s.
A towering matriarch figure whose voice defined her genre.

artists.name: Bessie Smith
artists.summary: The best-selling blues singer of the 1920s, known as the Empress of the Blues. Her power and phrasing shaped generations of jazz, blues and soul singers.
know: Her 1923 debut record Downhearted Blues was a huge seller for Columbia.
She recorded St. Louis Blues with Louis Armstrong on cornet in 1925.
Janis Joplin helped pay for a headstone on her unmarked grave in 1970.
keyAlbums: Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out (Columbia single)
songs: Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out

influencedBy.why: Toured in the same minstrel troupe as a teenager and absorbed Rainey's stagecraft and big-voiced delivery.

cousins.why: Defining female voice of her genre whose phrasing set the standard.
Regal, powerhouse singer crowned royalty of her genre.

artists.name: Charley Patton
artists.summary: Often called the father of the Delta blues, he was the region's most popular early performer. His rough voice, percussive guitar and showmanship shaped the next wave of Delta players.
know: He was based for years around Dockery Plantation, a hub for early Delta musicians.
He first recorded for Paramount in 1929.
He was known for showman tricks like playing guitar behind his back and between his knees.
keyAlbums: Screamin' and Hollerin' the Blues: The Worlds of Charley Patton

cousins.why: Founding father figure of his genre on late-1920s records.
Early pioneer whose records captured a regional style at its source.

artists.name: Blind Lemon Jefferson
artists.summary: One of the first male blues stars on record and a defining voice of Texas blues. His free, single-note guitar runs and high voice influenced players across the South.
know: He was one of the best-selling male blues recording artists of the 1920s, mostly on Paramount.
He played on the streets of Dallas's Deep Ellum district.
He died in Chicago in December 1929 under unclear circumstances.
keyAlbums: See That My Grave Is Kept Clean (Paramount single)
songs: See That My Grave Is Kept Clean

cousins.why: Rambling solo singer-guitarist who became an early record star.
Wandering street-corner troubadour of his genre.

artists.name: Mississippi John Hurt
artists.summary: A gentle singer and fingerpicker whose 1928 recordings and 1960s rediscovery made him a hero of the folk revival. His warm, rolling guitar style is still a model for acoustic players.
know: He recorded for OKeh in 1928 and then returned to farming for decades.
A fan tracked him down in 1963 using the hometown named in one of his old songs.
He played the Newport Folk Festival in 1963 after his rediscovery.

cousins.why: Homespun, melodic picking and singing rooted in old songs.
Soft-spoken voice over intricate fingerpicked guitar.

artists.name: King Oliver
artists.summary: A cornet leader whose Creole Jazz Band made some of the first great jazz records and who mentored Louis Armstrong.
know: His 1923 Creole Jazz Band sessions are among the most important early jazz recordings.
He was known for using mutes and plungers to make his horn growl and talk.
He brought a young Louis Armstrong from New Orleans to Chicago as second cornet in 1922.

cousins.why: A bandleader who shaped a city scene and trained the next generation of stars.
A bandleader whose group became the training ground for a genre's next stars.

artists.name: Louis Armstrong
artists.summary: The trumpeter and singer who turned jazz into a soloist's art and taught popular singers how to swing.
know: His Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings of the late 1920s set the standard for jazz soloing.
He helped popularize scat singing, using wordless syllables like a horn line.
He played trumpet on a 1930 Jimmie Rodgers record, an early meeting of jazz and country.

influencedBy.why: Treated Oliver as his mentor and played second cornet in his Creole Jazz Band from 1922.

cousins.why: A defining popular voice who made relaxed, swinging phrasing the norm for singers.
A player who turned his instrument into the lead voice of a new popular style.

artists.name: Bix Beiderbecke
artists.summary: A self taught cornetist whose clear, lyrical tone offered a cooler alternative to hot trumpet and pointed toward later cool jazz.
know: He was largely self taught and read music poorly, learning by ear from records.
His recordings with saxophonist Frankie Trumbauer, especially Singin' the Blues, were studied by many horn players.
He died at 28, and his brief career became one of jazz's first tragic legends.

influencedBy.why: Heard Armstrong playing on Mississippi riverboats as a teenager and was deeply impressed by his playing.

cousins.why: A gentle, introspective stylist who died young and was mythologized afterward.
A gifted, short lived talent whose small output became legendary.

artists.name: Duke Ellington
artists.summary: The most important composer in jazz, who wrote for the specific voices of his band members for half a century.
know: His orchestra's residency at Harlem's Cotton Club from 1927 made him nationally famous.
He worked closely with composer Billy Strayhorn, who wrote Take the A Train for the band.
His 1956 Newport Jazz Festival set revived his career and put him on the cover of Time.
songs: It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing)

cousins.why: A composer and bandleader of huge range who saluted Ellington by name in Sir Duke.
A composer who led a band and wrote parts around the strengths of individual players.

artists.name: The Carter Family
artists.summary: A family trio of A.P., Sara and Maybelle Carter whose recordings built the core songbook of country music. Maybelle's guitar playing became a standard technique for generations.
know: They first recorded at the 1927 Bristol Sessions for producer Ralph Peer.
Maybelle Carter's thumb-led melody style became known as the Carter scratch.
A.P. Carter traveled through Appalachia collecting old songs, often with Black guitarist Lesley Riddle.
keyAlbums: Anchored in Love: Their Complete Victor Recordings 1927–1928
songs: I'm Thinking Tonight of My Blue Eyes

cousins.why: Among the first recordings to define a whole regional tradition, as the Carters did for country.
An early recording star who turned older folk material into a genre's foundation.

artists.name: Jimmie Rodgers
artists.summary: Often called the Father of Country Music, Rodgers mixed hillbilly songs, blues and a trademark yodel into country's first solo star persona. His records shaped nearly every country singer of the next generation.
know: He recorded his first sides at the 1927 Bristol Sessions, the same week as the Carter Family.
In 1930 he recorded "Blue Yodel No. 9" with Louis Armstrong on trumpet.
He was one of the first three inductees into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1961.

cousins.why: A rambling singer who died young and left a small catalog that defined his genre.
The first big solo recording star of her genre, as Rodgers was for country.

artists.name: Son House
artists.summary: A fierce singer and slide guitarist whose intensity made him a direct teacher figure for Robert Johnson and Muddy Waters. His 1960s rediscovery brought raw Delta blues to new audiences.
know: He was a preacher before turning to blues and wrestled with that conflict all his life.
Alan Lomax recorded him for the Library of Congress in 1941 and 1942.
He was rediscovered living in Rochester, New York in 1964.

influencedBy.why: Traveled and played with Patton, who brought him along to his 1930 Paramount session.

cousins.why: Stark, stomping guitar and voice with almost nothing else.
Sin-and-salvation intensity from a deeply religious performer.

artists.name: Robert Johnson
artists.summary: His small body of recordings became the most influential in blues once reissued in 1961. His guitar technique and songs fed directly into Chicago blues and British blues rock.
know: He recorded only 29 songs, in sessions in San Antonio in 1936 and Dallas in 1937.
Legend says he sold his soul at a crossroads, a story attached to him after his death.
He died at 27 near Greenwood, Mississippi.
keyAlbums: King of the Delta Blues Singers
King of the Delta Blues Singers, Vol. II

influencedBy.why: Hung around Son House's shows as a young man and copied his slide playing and intensity.
Reworked James's 22-20 Blues into his own 32-20 Blues.
Grew up in the Delta scene Patton defined and drew on its rhythmic style.

cousins.why: Doomed young legend whose small catalog defined a genre.
Obscure in life, hugely influential after his early death.

artists.name: Skip James
artists.summary: A haunting falsetto singer with an eerie minor-key guitar style unlike anyone else in the Delta. His 1931 recordings and 1960s comeback made him a cult figure for rock musicians.
know: He often played in an open D minor tuning, giving his songs a dark sound.
He recorded for Paramount in 1931, then left music for decades.
Royalties from Cream's cover of I'm So Glad helped him pay medical bills.

cousins.why: Hushed, haunting voice over unusual guitar tunings.
Otherworldly falsetto and spellbinding solo performances.

artists.name: Lead Belly
artists.summary: A 12-string guitar powerhouse whose vast songbook bridged blues, folk and work songs. His songs became standards for the folk revival, skiffle and grunge alike.
know: John and Alan Lomax recorded him at Louisiana's Angola prison in 1933.
His signature instrument was a loud 12-string guitar.
The Weavers had a huge hit with Goodnight, Irene in 1950, a year after his death.
songs: Where Did You Sleep Last Night

influencedBy.why: Worked as Jefferson's guide and playing partner around Dallas, learning his songs and runs.

cousins.why: Folk songbook keeper who carried hundreds of traditional songs.
Turned the same folk and work songs into a pop craze.

artists.name: Fats Waller
artists.summary: A virtuoso stride pianist and comic entertainer who wrote enduring standards and brought joy and wit to jazz.
know: He wrote Ain't Misbehavin' and Honeysuckle Rose, both still widely played.
He was also a skilled pipe organist and recorded jazz on the organ early on.
His group Fats Waller and His Rhythm made hundreds of records in the 1930s.

cousins.why: A jovial piano man who made rolling piano the center of a popular style.
A showman pianist whose playing was as entertaining as it was skilled.

artists.name: Art Tatum
artists.summary: A nearly blind pianist whose speed and harmonic daring set a technical bar that every jazz pianist after him measured against.
know: He had very limited eyesight from childhood and learned much by ear.
His rich reharmonizations of standards influenced bebop musicians, including Charlie Parker.
Late in life he recorded a huge series of solo and group sessions for producer Norman Granz.

influencedBy.why: Named Waller as his main early model, and Waller in turn famously praised Tatum as the greater player.

cousins.why: A virtuoso who redrew the limits of what his instrument could do.
A technical wizard whose dazzling speed set a new standard for his instrument.

artists.name: Count Basie
artists.summary: A bandleader and pianist whose light, riff driven Kansas City swing defined how a big band could groove.
know: His sparse piano style left space and let the rhythm section breathe.
His late 1930s rhythm section of Freddie Green, Walter Page and Jo Jones is legendary for its smooth pulse.
He became the first African American man to win a Grammy, in 1958.

influencedBy.why: Picked up informal organ lessons from Waller in Harlem during the 1920s.

cousins.why: A dance band leader who built swing into another regional style.
A bandleader whose tight, riff based groove machine kept dancers moving.

artists.name: Benny Goodman
artists.summary: The clarinetist and bandleader known as the King of Swing, who brought swing to a mass audience and integrated his bands.
know: His 1938 Carnegie Hall concert was a landmark for jazz in a classical concert hall.
He led one of the first prominent racially integrated groups, with Teddy Wilson and Lionel Hampton.
He hired guitarist Charlie Christian in 1939 and gave him a national stage.
keyAlbums: The Famous 1938 Carnegie Hall Jazz Concert

cousins.why: A crowned king who brought a Black-rooted style to a huge mainstream audience.
A bandleader who made swing the dance music of another tradition.

artists.name: Billie Holiday
artists.summary: A singer who phrased like a horn player and turned her small voice into one of the most emotionally direct instruments in music.
know: Lester Young nicknamed her Lady Day, and she called him Prez.
Her 1939 recording of Strange Fruit, a song protesting lynching, became a landmark of protest music.
She was raised largely in Baltimore and began singing in Harlem clubs as a teenager.

influencedBy.why: Named Bessie Smith as one of her two main early models for vocal power and feeling.
Said she wanted Armstrong's feel and borrowed his way of bending melodies.
Recorded and toured with Young in the 1930s, and their phrasing grew together.

cousins.why: A singer whose behind-the-beat phrasing and raw delivery owed a lot to Holiday.
A singer with a distinctive, conversational phrasing rooted in jazz vocals.
A pop singer who learned phrasing and intimacy from Holiday.

artists.name: Coleman Hawkins
artists.summary: The man who made the tenor saxophone a serious jazz solo voice and later championed the young bebop players.
know: His 1939 Body and Soul is a famous improvisation that barely states the melody.
He led a 1944 session with Dizzy Gillespie often called the first bebop recording.
He hired Thelonious Monk when few others would.

influencedBy.why: Sat next to Armstrong in Fletcher Henderson's band in 1924 and picked up his rhythmic drive.
Widely credited with absorbing Tatum's harmonic richness into his own chord-based soloing.

cousins.why: A pioneer who established his instrument as the lead solo voice of a genre.
A player whose singing tone made his instrument the main solo voice in his style.

artists.name: Lester Young
artists.summary: A tenor saxophonist whose airy tone and floating lines offered an alternative to Hawkins and laid the path for cool jazz and bebop.
know: He became a star in Count Basie's band in the late 1930s.
Billie Holiday called him Prez, short for President of the tenor sax.
He was known for coining hip slang and wearing a pork pie hat, later honored by Mingus.
keyAlbums: The President Plays with the Oscar Peterson Trio

influencedBy.why: Cited the light tone on Beiderbecke's records with Frankie Trumbauer as a model for his sound.
Played tenor in Basie's band, where the relaxed rhythm section shaped his floating swing.

cousins.why: An understated stylist whose softness carried deep feeling.
A musician whose relaxed, behind-the-beat feel changed how a genre swings.

artists.name: Django Reinhardt
artists.summary: A Romani guitarist who created a European jazz style and became one of the first great jazz soloists from outside America.
know: A fire left two fingers on his fretting hand badly damaged, and he built a new technique around it.
He co-led the Quintette du Hot Club de France with violinist Stéphane Grappelli.
He toured the United States with Duke Ellington in 1946.

influencedBy.why: Was reportedly overwhelmed on first hearing Armstrong records around 1931 and turned toward jazz.
Admired Ellington's music and toured America as a guest with his orchestra in 1946.

cousins.why: Tony Iommi kept playing after losing fingertips, inspired by Reinhardt's story.
A guitarist whose melodic picking draws openly on Reinhardt's style.

artists.name: Bob Wills
artists.summary: Bandleader of the Texas Playboys who fused fiddle music with jazz, blues and big band swing. He made country into dance music and brought drums and electric steel guitar into the genre.
know: His trademark onstage holler was "Ah-haaa!"
He got his start with the Light Crust Doughboys in Fort Worth in the early 1930s.
Merle Haggard and Waylon Jennings both made records honoring him.

influencedBy.why: Wills often told of riding about 50 miles on horseback to see Bessie Smith perform, and blues was a core part of his repertoire.
As a young performer Wills sang Jimmie Rodgers songs, and Rodgers' blend of blues and country was a model for his own.

cousins.why: A swing bandleader whose job was keeping a dance floor full.
Led a big swing dance band that made his genre popular across America.

artists.name: Bing Crosby
artists.summary: Bing Crosby pioneered the relaxed, intimate crooning style that the electric microphone made possible. He was the best-selling recording star of the first half of the 20th century.
know: His recording of 'White Christmas' is often cited as the best-selling single of all time.
He started out as one of the Rhythm Boys with Paul Whiteman's Orchestra in the late 1920s.
He invested in Ampex and helped bring magnetic tape recording into radio broadcasting.
songs: Where the Blue of the Night
Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?

influencedBy.why: Crosby repeatedly credited Armstrong as his main musical influence and borrowed his swinging, conversational phrasing.
As Whiteman bandmates in the late 1920s, Crosby absorbed Beiderbecke's jazz feel and the two were close friends.

cousins.why: Another warm, effortless crooner who made the microphone feel like a private conversation.
The first mass-media star of country music, as Crosby was for mainstream pop.

artists.name: T-Bone Walker
artists.summary: The pioneer of electric blues guitar, he combined jazzy single-note lines with horn-band swing. Nearly every later electric blues guitarist traces back to his sound.
know: He was among the first bluesmen to record on electric guitar, in the early 1940s.
He was a showman who played guitar behind his head and did the splits.
As a boy in Dallas he guided Blind Lemon Jefferson around the streets.
songs: Call It Stormy Monday (But Tuesday Is Just as Bad)

influencedBy.why: Led Jefferson around Dallas as a boy and soaked up his playing up close.

cousins.why: Fellow Texas-born electric guitar pioneer who made the instrument a lead voice.
Flashy guitar showman who borrowed T-Bone's stagecraft for rock and roll.

artists.name: John Lee Hooker
artists.summary: A Mississippi-born singer whose hypnotic, one-chord boogie became his trademark in Detroit. His driving groove influenced rock bands from the 1960s onward.
know: His 1948 debut Boogie Chillen' topped the R&B chart.
He recorded under many pseudonyms for different labels in his early years.
His 1989 album The Healer revived his career and won a Grammy.
songs: One Bourbon, One Scotch, One Beer

cousins.why: Trance-like grooves built on a single repeating pattern.
Built hits on a relentless one-chord groove.

artists.name: Sister Rosetta Tharpe
artists.summary: A gospel star who played electrified guitar with blues bite, she is often called the godmother of rock and roll. Her guitar playing and showmanship anticipated rock decades early.
know: Her 1944 recording Strange Things Happening Every Day crossed over to the race records chart.
She played electric guitar with a style that later rock players echoed.
She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018.
keyAlbums: Strange Things Happening Every Day (Decca single)

cousins.why: Electric guitar showmanship that defined rock and roll.
Church-born fire carried into secular rock and roll.

artists.name: Louis Jordan
artists.summary: The bandleader and saxophonist who ruled 1940s R&B with witty, danceable jump blues. His small-combo shuffle rhythms were a direct blueprint for rock and roll.
know: He led a small group called the Tympany Five.
Choo Choo Ch'Boogie spent many weeks at number one on the R&B chart in 1946.
He was nicknamed the King of the Jukebox.
keyAlbums: Let the Good Times Roll: The Complete Decca Recordings 1938–1954
songs: Is You Is or Is You Ain't My Baby

cousins.why: Comic, crowd-pleasing entertainer who was also a serious musician.
Witty storytelling hits over a bouncing shuffle beat.

artists.name: Charlie Christian
artists.summary: The guitarist who made the amplified guitar a front-line jazz solo instrument and helped seed bebop before dying at 25.
know: Benny Goodman hired him in 1939 after hearing him play.
He jammed at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem, where bebop was taking shape.
He grew up in Oklahoma City and died of tuberculosis in 1942.
keyAlbums: The Genius of the Electric Guitar

influencedBy.why: Shaped his long horn-like guitar lines on the way Young phrased on tenor.
Joined Goodman's sextet in 1939, gaining the platform where his style matured.

cousins.why: A fellow Texas-born electric guitar pioneer who did the same for blues.
A guitarist who put the electric guitar at the front of a new genre.

artists.name: Charlie Parker
artists.summary: The alto saxophonist known as Bird who, with Gillespie, created bebop and rewrote the language of jazz improvisation.
know: He grew up in Kansas City, where he studied local players and memorized records.
His nickname Bird inspired the club name Birdland and many tune titles.
His struggles with heroin cut his life short at 34.

influencedBy.why: Memorized Young's solos from Basie records note for note as a teenager.
Worked in a New York restaurant where Tatum played and absorbed his harmonic speed.
Developed bebop alongside Gillespie in the early 1940s, trading ideas nightly.
Studied Hawkins's chord-based approach to improvising through the changes.

cousins.why: A virtuoso who rewrote his instrument's vocabulary and died young.
An artist who reinvented rhythmic phrasing in his medium.

artists.name: Dizzy Gillespie
artists.summary: A co-founder of bebop and a brilliant trumpeter and teacher who also fused jazz with Cuban rhythms.
know: He played a trumpet with an upturned bell and was known for puffed-out cheeks.
He hired Cuban conga player Chano Pozo in 1947, a key step for Afro-Cuban jazz.
He was a generous mentor who explained bebop harmony to many younger players.

influencedBy.why: Partnered with Parker to build bebop, crediting him for much of its rhythmic language.
Worked out new harmonies with Monk in after-hours sessions at Minton's.
Played on Hawkins's 1944 sessions, an early recorded home for bebop.

cousins.why: A bandleader at the center of the Latin side of the jazz and Cuban fusion.
A horn-playing bandleader who fused jazz with another rhythmic tradition.

artists.name: Thelonious Monk
artists.summary: A pianist and composer with a uniquely angular style whose tunes are among the most played in jazz.
know: He was house pianist at Minton's Playhouse during the birth of bebop.
His 1957 run at the Five Spot with John Coltrane is legendary.
He appeared on the cover of Time magazine in 1964.

influencedBy.why: Admired Ellington's piano and writing and devoted a full 1955 album to his tunes.
Got his first major recording work in Hawkins's 1944 group.

cousins.why: An idiosyncratic writer whose off-kilter angles became a style of their own.
A producer whose deliberately uneven timing became a signature.

artists.name: Ella Fitzgerald
artists.summary: The First Lady of Song, whose pure tone, perfect pitch and scat improvising made her the definitive interpreter of the American songbook.
know: She won an amateur night at Harlem's Apollo Theater in 1934 and soon joined Chick Webb's band.
Her Song Book albums for Verve covered the work of major American songwriters one by one.
She won the first Grammy for female vocal performance in 1958.
keyAlbums: Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Cole Porter Song Book
Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Duke Ellington Song Book

influencedBy.why: Drew on Armstrong's scat singing and later recorded duet albums with him.
Toured with Gillespie's big band in the late 1940s and brought bebop lines into her scat.

cousins.why: A definitive interpreter of the American songbook in pop.
A singer whose technical command made her the reference point for her genre.

artists.name: Nat King Cole
artists.summary: A top jazz pianist who led an influential trio and then became one of the best loved pop singers of his era.
know: His drummerless trio of piano, guitar and bass was widely imitated.
He hosted a national TV show in 1956, rare for a Black performer at the time.
His daughter Natalie Cole later topped charts with a virtual duet on Unforgettable.

cousins.why: A pianist-singer who modeled his early style closely on Cole.
A silky crossover singer who brought a Black vocal style to the pop mainstream.

artists.name: Frank Sinatra
artists.summary: Frank Sinatra turned the pop standard into a vehicle for adult storytelling. His 1950s Capitol albums with arrangers like Nelson Riddle helped invent the concept album.
know: He sang with the Harry James and Tommy Dorsey bands before going solo in 1942.
He won an Academy Award for his acting role in From Here to Eternity (1953).
He founded his own label, Reprise Records, in 1960.
songs: I've Got You Under My Skin

influencedBy.why: Sinatra decided to become a singer after seeing Crosby perform, and Crosby was his early model.
Sinatra called Holiday the greatest single musical influence on his singing, especially her phrasing.

cousins.why: Country's definitive interpreter of heartbreak, the way Sinatra was for the American songbook.
The other great interpreter of the Great American Songbook in the same era.

artists.name: Bill Monroe
artists.summary: Mandolinist and singer who created bluegrass with his Blue Grass Boys, the band that gave the genre its name. His fast, tight ensemble sound and high lonesome vocals set the template for the style.
know: Bluegrass music is named after his band, the Blue Grass Boys.
Elvis Presley covered his "Blue Moon of Kentucky" on his first Sun single in 1954.
He learned from his fiddler uncle Pendleton Vandiver, the subject of "Uncle Pen", and Black blues guitarist Arnold Shultz.

influencedBy.why: Monroe auditioned for the Grand Ole Opry in 1939 with Rodgers' "Mule Skinner Blues", and his early yodeling style drew on Rodgers.

cousins.why: A virtuoso who invented a fast, demanding new language for his genre.
Built the definitive band sound of his genre and trained many of its later stars.

artists.name: Hank Williams
artists.summary: The most influential songwriter in country music, whose plain, emotional songs about heartbreak became the genre's standard. He died at 29 but wrote much of the country canon.
know: He died on January 1, 1953, in the back seat of his car on the way to a show.
He learned music as a boy from Black street singer Rufus "Tee-Tot" Payne.
He also recorded moral recitations under the alias Luke the Drifter.
songs: I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry

influencedBy.why: Williams' blues-based songs and yodel breaks, as on "Lovesick Blues", follow the style Rodgers set.

cousins.why: Died young and left songs that became the backbone of his genre.
A singer whose raw emotional delivery and troubled life became legend.

artists.name: Woody Guthrie
artists.summary: Songwriter who chronicled the Dust Bowl, migrant workers and labor struggles, and became the model for the American political folk singer. Bob Dylan and a whole folk revival grew from his work.
know: His guitar carried a sign reading "This machine kills fascists."
He wrote "This Land Is Your Land" in 1940 as a reply to "God Bless America."
Huntington's disease ended his career in the 1950s, and he died in 1967.

influencedBy.why: He set many of his lyrics to Carter Family melodies; "This Land Is Your Land" borrows from their "When the World's on Fire."
His early songs and singing followed the Jimmie Rodgers style popular in Texas and Oklahoma.
He became close friends with Lead Belly in New York and the two performed together.

cousins.why: Used songs as direct political commentary for working people.
Wrote songs of struggle that became anthems for the dispossessed.

artists.name: Muddy Waters
artists.summary: He plugged Delta blues into an amplifier and built the Chicago blues band sound. His records inspired the Rolling Stones, British blues and much of rock.
know: Alan Lomax first recorded him at Stovall Plantation in Mississippi in 1941.
The Rolling Stones took their name from one of his songs.
His 1977 album Hard Again, produced by Johnny Winter, won a Grammy.

influencedBy.why: Watched House play around Clarksdale and said he modeled his slide style on him.
Said Johnson's records hit him hard and studied his songs and guitar.
Grew up in the Delta tradition Patton led and absorbed its rhythms.

cousins.why: Swaggering electric band that took his sound worldwide.
Commanding bandleader who ran a tight, groove-driven band.

artists.name: Howlin' Wolf
artists.summary: A towering performer with a ferocious, gravelly voice who brought raw Delta power to Chicago. His Chess records became staples of British and American rock bands.
know: He first recorded with Sam Phillips in Memphis before moving to Chicago and Chess.
He appeared on the TV show Shindig! in 1965 at the Rolling Stones' request.
He was a big man, about six foot three, with a famously imposing stage presence.

influencedBy.why: Learned guitar from Patton around Dockery Plantation and copied his showmanship.
Tried to imitate Rodgers's yodel and said it turned into his howl.

cousins.why: Growling, untamed voice over jagged music.
Raw, roaring frontman energy with no polish.

artists.name: B.B. King
artists.summary: The most famous ambassador of the blues, known for expressive string bends and vibrato on his guitar Lucille. He took blues into concert halls worldwide for six decades.
know: He named his guitars Lucille after a dance hall fire in Arkansas started by a fight over a woman of that name.
He was a DJ on Memphis radio station WDIA, where the nickname Blues Boy began.
The Thrill Is Gone in 1969 became his biggest crossover hit.
songs: Every Day I Have the Blues

influencedBy.why: Said hearing T-Bone's electric guitar made him want to play one himself.
Listened to Jefferson's records as a boy and named him an early favorite.
Cited Django's melodic, singing lines as a model for his solos.
Named Christian's jazz single-note style as a key guitar influence.

cousins.why: Beloved global ambassador for his genre.
Southern singer who carried his music into the mainstream.

artists.name: Willie Dixon
artists.summary: Chess Records' house bassist, producer and chief songwriter, he wrote many of the best-known Chicago blues songs. His songs became core repertoire for British and American rock bands.
know: He won an Illinois Golden Gloves heavyweight boxing title in 1937.
He wrote hits for Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf and Little Walter at Chess.
He settled a lawsuit with Led Zeppelin over Whole Lotta Love in 1985.
songs: I Just Want to Make Love to You

cousins.why: Songwriter behind a string of other artists' hits.
Label house band and studio backbone shaping a whole sound.

artists.name: Little Walter
artists.summary: He reinvented the harmonica by cupping it to a microphone and playing through an amp like a saxophone. Every modern blues harp player builds on his sound.
know: His instrumental Juke reached number one on the R&B chart in 1952.
He played in Muddy Waters's band before going solo.
He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2008, a first for a harmonica player.

influencedBy.why: Wanted the harmonica to sound like Jordan's jumping saxophone lines.
Honed his amplified band style as a member of Muddy's group.

cousins.why: Revolutionized what his instrument could say.
Used amplification as part of the instrument itself.

artists.name: Elmore James
artists.summary: The King of the Slide Guitar, famous for a loud, ringing slide riff that opens Dust My Broom. His amplified slide sound shaped blues rock guitar.
know: His 1951 version of Dust My Broom became a hit and his signature.
He worked repairing radios and tinkered with his amplified sound.
Brian Jones of the Rolling Stones briefly called himself Elmo Lewis in tribute.
keyAlbums: The Sky Is Crying: The History of Elmore James

influencedBy.why: Built his signature hit on Johnson's I Believe I'll Dust My Broom and its slide riff.

cousins.why: Slide guitar as the lead voice of a hard-driving band.
Fuzzy, stomping slide riffs in a raw garage setting.

artists.name: Jimmy Reed
artists.summary: His lazy, loping shuffles and high harmonica made him one of the best-selling bluesmen of the 1950s. His simple, catchy songs were easy for young rock bands to learn and cover.
know: His boyhood friend Eddie Taylor played guitar on many of his records.
His wife, known as Mama Reed, often sang along and fed him lyrics in the studio.
He scored more pop chart crossovers than most of his Chicago peers.
songs: Baby What You Want Me to Do

cousins.why: Simple, chugging grooves that made hits feel effortless.
Built early sets on the same easy, rolling shuffle.

artists.name: Mahalia Jackson
artists.summary: The Queen of Gospel, whose huge voice brought gospel to mainstream audiences. She was a key voice of the civil rights movement.
know: Move On Up a Little Higher in 1947 was a massive seller for gospel.
She sang at the 1963 March on Washington before Martin Luther King Jr. spoke.
She recorded with Duke Ellington on Black, Brown and Beige in 1958.
songs: Move On Up a Little Higher

influencedBy.why: Grew up listening to Bessie's records and credited her phrasing even while singing only sacred music.

cousins.why: Church-trained powerhouse who sang at her funeral.
Gospel star whose voice reshaped popular music.

artists.name: Miles Davis
artists.summary: A trumpeter and bandleader who reinvented jazz several times, from cool and modal jazz to electric fusion.
know: Kind of Blue is the best-selling album in jazz history.
He joined Charlie Parker's quintet as a teenager in the mid 1940s.
His bands launched the careers of Coltrane, Bill Evans, Herbie Hancock and many others.

influencedBy.why: Idolized Gillespie as a teen and modeled his early bebop trumpet on him.
Played in Parker's quintet from 1945 and learned bebop on the bandstand.
Acknowledged Armstrong as the root of all modern trumpet playing.
Learned harmony from Monk in New York and made 'Round Midnight a signature.
Openly revered Ellington and recorded the long tribute He Loved Him Madly after his death.
Credited Evans's modal and impressionist voicings for shaping the sound of Kind of Blue.
Was drawn to Hendrix's electric sound and planned to record with him before his death.
Cited Sly Stone's funk as a model for his late 1960s and 1970s electric bands.
Took James Brown's rhythm-first funk as a blueprint for On the Corner.

cousins.why: An artist defined by constant reinvention across decades.
Cited Bitches Brew as an influence on the mood of OK Computer.
A restless genre-crossing bandleader who was also a friend and admirer.

artists.name: John Coltrane
artists.summary: A saxophonist who pushed harmony and intensity to new limits and turned jazz toward spiritual searching.
know: His dense rapid style was nicknamed sheets of sound by critic Ira Gitler.
A Love Supreme is a four-part devotional suite and one of jazz's best known albums.
He named his son Ravi after the sitar player Ravi Shankar.

influencedBy.why: Started on alto and tenor studying Young's lyrical phrasing.
Cited Hawkins's chord-based tenor style as a foundation for his harmonic approach.
Said hearing Parker changed his life and set him on the bebop path.
Played in Gillespie's band from 1949 to 1951.
Was a member of Davis's quintet and sextet, absorbing his modal approach on Kind of Blue.
Played in Monk's quartet in 1957 and credited him with teaching him new harmonic ideas.
Studied Indian music, met Shankar, and drew on raga ideas for his drones and modes.

cousins.why: Their Eight Miles High guitar lines were directly inspired by Coltrane.
A guitarist whose spiritual searching led him to record music from A Love Supreme.
A rapper who has said he built his flow on Coltrane's phrasing.

artists.name: Charles Mingus
artists.summary: A virtuoso bassist and fiery composer who blended gospel, blues, bebop and free playing into vivid large works.
know: He was raised in the Watts neighborhood of Los Angeles.
He wrote Goodbye Pork Pie Hat as an elegy for Lester Young.
Joni Mitchell made a full album of collaborations with him near the end of his life.
keyAlbums: The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady
songs: Better Git It in Your Soul

influencedBy.why: Called Ellington his idol and briefly played in his band in 1953.
Played bass in Armstrong's band in the early 1940s.
Played with Parker, including the 1953 Massey Hall concert, and absorbed bebop language.

cousins.why: A composer-bandleader who mixed genres into ambitious, demanding works.
A songwriter who pushed her genre into jazz and collaborated with Mingus.

artists.name: Sonny Rollins
artists.summary: A tenor saxophonist famous for long, witty, thematic improvisations and one of the last giants of the bebop era.
know: He famously took a break in 1959 and practiced on the Williamsburg Bridge, leading to his album The Bridge.
His Saxophone Colossus is one of the most celebrated jazz albums.
He played the sax solo on the Rolling Stones' Waiting on a Friend.
keyAlbums: A Night at the Village Vanguard

influencedBy.why: Grew up idolizing Hawkins and later recorded Sonny Meets Hawk! with him.
Played alongside Parker on a Miles Davis session and called him a primary influence.
Was mentored by Monk as a teenager in Harlem and recorded with him.
Was a key member of Davis's groups in the early 1950s.

cousins.why: A band built around long, exploratory live improvisation.
Rollins brought his tenor voice to their recording of Waiting on a Friend.

artists.name: Art Blakey
artists.summary: A powerhouse drummer whose Jazz Messengers defined hard bop and served for decades as a school for young stars.
know: His Jazz Messengers launched Lee Morgan, Wayne Shorter, Freddie Hubbard and Wynton Marsalis among many others.
His press rolls and driving cymbal beat became hard bop signatures.
He played in Billy Eckstine's 1940s big band alongside Parker and Gillespie.

influencedBy.why: Played on Monk's early Blue Note sessions and called him a key musical mentor.
Shared the bandstand with Gillespie in Billy Eckstine's bebop big band.
Played next to Parker in the Eckstine band and absorbed bebop's rhythmic language.

cousins.why: A demanding bandleader whose group trained a generation of players.
A rhythm-driven group whose drumming defined a city's groove.

artists.name: Dave Brubeck
artists.summary: A pianist whose quartet brought jazz to college campuses and made odd time signatures a hit.
know: Time Out was built around unusual meters and became a million seller.
Take Five was written by his alto player Paul Desmond.
He studied composition with French composer Darius Milhaud.

influencedBy.why: Admired Ellington deeply and wrote the tribute tune The Duke.

cousins.why: A band that made odd time signatures popular with a wide audience.
A group that built complex meters into accessible music.

artists.name: Bill Evans
artists.summary: A pianist whose impressionist harmony and interactive trio changed jazz piano and shaped the sound of Kind of Blue.
know: He played on Miles Davis's Kind of Blue and wrote its liner notes.
His trio with bassist Scott LaFaro treated bass, drums and piano as equal voices.
His Village Vanguard sets of June 1961 were recorded days before LaFaro died.

influencedBy.why: Played in Davis's sextet in 1958 and 1959, developing his modal voicings in that setting.
Named Cole's piano playing as an early model for his touch.

cousins.why: An artist whose atmospheric, harmonic textures create mood over drive.
A quiet, introspective stylist whose music feels intimate and unhurried.

artists.name: Ornette Coleman
artists.summary: An alto saxophonist who freed jazz from fixed chord changes and opened the door to free jazz.
know: His album Free Jazz gave the movement its name.
He played a plastic alto saxophone early in his career.
He started out playing in Texas rhythm and blues bands.
keyAlbums: The Shape of Jazz to Come

influencedBy.why: Studied Parker's bebop closely as a young player before breaking away from fixed changes.

cousins.why: A band that, like Coleman, threw out the rulebook; Lou Reed cited him.
A group that built music on freedom, noise and unconventional structure.

artists.name: Sun Ra
artists.summary: A visionary bandleader who claimed to come from Saturn and fused big band swing, free jazz and electronics into cosmic theater.
know: His Arkestra lived and rehearsed together, especially in Chicago and later Philadelphia.
He was among the first jazz musicians to use electronic keyboards like the Moog.
He ran his own label, El Saturn, decades before independent labels were common in jazz.
keyAlbums: The Heliocentric Worlds of Sun Ra

influencedBy.why: Loved Ellington's orchestra and carried its rich big band voicing into the Arkestra.

cousins.why: A collective that built a cosmic Afrofuturist mythology around funk.
A producer who carries cosmic, spiritual jazz ideas into electronic music.
A Detroit rock band that openly championed Sun Ra and shared bills with him.

artists.name: Lefty Frizzell
artists.summary: Honky-tonk singer whose smooth, rolling way of stretching syllables changed how country singers phrased a line. Haggard, Jones, Nelson and Strait all drew on him.
know: In 1951 he had four songs in the country top 10 at the same time.
He was the first to record "Long Black Veil" in 1959.
He released a full album of Jimmie Rodgers songs in 1951.
songs: If You've Got the Money I've Got the Time
I Love You a Thousand Ways

influencedBy.why: Rodgers was his boyhood idol, and he recorded a tribute album of Rodgers songs in 1951.

cousins.why: A singer's singer whose phrasing other vocalists studied and copied.
Set the standard for phrasing in his genre.

artists.name: Patsy Cline
artists.summary: A rich-voiced singer who brought country into pop with polished Nashville sound ballads. She remains one of the most admired vocalists in country history.
know: She broke through by winning Arthur Godfrey's Talent Scouts in 1957 with "Walkin' After Midnight."
"Crazy" was written by a young Willie Nelson.
She died in a plane crash in March 1963 at age 30.

influencedBy.why: She recorded Wills songs including "San Antonio Rose" and "Faded Love."
She recorded Hank Williams songs such as "Lovesick Blues" and "Your Cheatin' Heart."

cousins.why: A powerhouse voice built for aching ballads.
A big, classic voice that crosses over to a mass pop audience.

artists.name: Johnny Cash
artists.summary: The Man in Black, whose deep voice and boom-chicka-boom rhythm made him a figure in country, rock and folk alike. His prison concerts and late-career American Recordings kept him relevant for five decades.
know: He started at Sun Records in Memphis in 1955 alongside Elvis Presley.
His 1968 album At Folsom Prison revived his career.
He married June Carter of the Carter Family in 1968.
keyAlbums: American IV: The Man Comes Around

influencedBy.why: He married June Carter, toured with Mother Maybelle and the Carter Sisters, and recorded Carter Family songs.
He recorded Hank Williams songs such as "You Win Again" and "I Could Never Be Ashamed of You" at Sun.
Rodgers' train songs and blue yodels were a clear model for Cash's early material.
Cash named Sister Rosetta Tharpe as one of his favorite singers growing up.
Cash championed Dylan, recorded his songs like "It Ain't Me Babe", and duetted with him on Nashville Skyline.

cousins.why: Writes plainspoken stories about working people and outsiders.
A huge, deep voice that carried authority and menace.

artists.name: Pete Seeger
artists.summary: Banjo player, singer and activist who carried Woody Guthrie's tradition into the 1950s and 60s folk revival. He wrote or popularized many of the era's anthems.
know: He was a member of the Almanac Singers with Woody Guthrie and later the Weavers.
He was blacklisted in the 1950s and convicted of contempt of Congress, a verdict later overturned.
The Byrds took his "Turn! Turn! Turn!" to number one in 1965.
keyAlbums: We Shall Overcome: The Complete Carnegie Hall Concert
songs: Where Have All the Flowers Gone?
Waist Deep in the Big Muddy

influencedBy.why: He traveled and performed with Guthrie, and they formed the Almanac Singers together.
He learned 12-string guitar from Lead Belly, and the Weavers' hit "Goodnight, Irene" was a Lead Belly song.

cousins.why: A teacher-activist figure who treats music as education.
A voice of the civil rights movement who sang its songs at rallies.

artists.name: Odetta
artists.summary: A singer with a powerful, classically trained voice who brought work songs, spirituals and blues to the folk revival. She inspired Dylan, Baez and a generation of folk singers.
know: She sang at the 1963 March on Washington.
Bob Dylan said hearing her record was the first thing that turned him on to folk music.
Martin Luther King Jr. called her the queen of American folk music.

influencedBy.why: She recorded many songs from Lead Belly's repertoire, including "Take This Hammer."
She recorded a full album of his songs, Odetta Sings Dylan, in 1965.

cousins.why: A deep, commanding voice tied to the civil rights movement.
A spiritual singer whose voice carried a movement.

artists.name: Lonnie Donegan
artists.summary: The King of Skiffle, whose upbeat take on American folk and blues set off a do-it-yourself guitar craze in 1950s Britain. Many future British rock stars started in skiffle bands because of him.
know: His 1955 recording of "Rock Island Line" was a hit in both the UK and the US.
John Lennon's first group, the Quarrymen, was a skiffle band inspired by him.
He took the name Lonnie from blues guitarist Lonnie Johnson.
songs: Does Your Chewing Gum Lose Its Flavour (On the Bedpost Overnight?)

influencedBy.why: His breakthrough "Rock Island Line" came from Lead Belly's version.
He recorded Guthrie songs such as "Grand Coulee Dam."

cousins.why: Made a generation believe anyone could pick up a guitar and start a band.
Sparked a youth movement that grew into a whole scene.

artists.name: Chuck Berry
artists.summary: Chuck Berry set the template for rock and roll guitar and songwriting in the 1950s. His riffs and teenage story songs were copied by nearly every rock band that followed.
know: His first hit, Maybellene, was adapted from the fiddle tune Ida Red.
Johnny B. Goode is on the golden record carried by the Voyager spacecraft.
He was in the first class inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1986.

influencedBy.why: Berry named T-Bone Walker as a key model for his electric guitar playing and stage moves.
Berry said he identified with Louis Jordan, and the Johnny B. Goode intro echoes a guitar line from a Jordan record.
Muddy Waters sent the young Berry to Leonard Chess, which led to his Chess Records contract.
Berry cited Charlie Christian's single-note electric jazz lines as an early guitar inspiration.
Maybellene grew out of Ida Red, a fiddle tune Bob Wills and his Texas Playboys had recorded.
Berry admired Nat King Cole's clear diction and aimed to sing just as plainly.

cousins.why: Both wrote the basic song vocabulary their genres still use.
Both pack vivid little teenage stories into tight, funny verses.

artists.name: Little Richard
artists.summary: Little Richard was one of rock and roll's founding performers, with a pounding piano, a shrieking voice and a flamboyant stage act. His mid-1950s hits defined the music's wild side.
know: Tutti Frutti began as a bawdy song he cleaned up in the studio in 1955.
Sister Rosetta Tharpe invited him to sing at her show in Macon when he was a teenager.
The Beatles opened for him in 1962 before they were famous.

influencedBy.why: Tharpe heard him sing before her 1947 Macon concert and brought him on stage, his first time performing for a big crowd.
He named Louis Jordan as a major early influence on his jump-blues style.
He cut his hits at Cosimo Matassa's New Orleans studio with the same session players behind Fats Domino's records.

cousins.why: Both were explosive Black showmen from Georgia who made the live performance the point.
Both mixed gospel shouting with flamboyant, gender-bending style.
Both treat outrageous costume and theatrics as part of the music.

artists.name: Fats Domino
artists.summary: Fats Domino brought New Orleans piano rhythm and blues into the early rock and roll mainstream. His relaxed rolling piano and warm voice made him one of the best-selling artists of the 1950s.
know: The Fat Man from 1949 is often called one of the first rock and roll records.
He sold more than 65 million records.
He was rescued by boat from his flooded home after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

influencedBy.why: His nickname was given by bandleader Billy Diamond in honor of piano men like Fats Waller.
His shuffling jump-blues rhythms follow the band sound Louis Jordan made popular in the 1940s.
His 1956 hit Blueberry Hill followed Louis Armstrong's 1949 recording of the song.

cousins.why: Both are pillars of the New Orleans groove.
Both have a warm, friendly voice over a loping beat, and Jamaican ska grew partly out of New Orleans R&B.

artists.name: Bo Diddley
artists.summary: Bo Diddley built songs on a single driving rhythm, the shave-and-a-haircut pattern now called the Bo Diddley beat. His rhythm-first approach and homemade guitars shaped rock, garage and punk.
know: He built his own rectangular guitars.
He took up violin as a child before switching to guitar.
He was banned from The Ed Sullivan Show in 1955 after playing a different song than agreed.

influencedBy.why: His one-chord, rhythm-driven songs follow John Lee Hooker's boogie approach.
He named Louis Jordan among the musicians he listened to growing up.
He came up in the same South Side Chicago scene as Muddy Waters and recorded for the same Chess family of labels.

cousins.why: Both put rhythm ahead of melody and chord changes.
Both build long songs on one hypnotic groove.

artists.name: Elvis Presley
artists.summary: Elvis Presley fused country, blues and gospel at Sun Records in Memphis and became rock and roll's first superstar. His records and TV appearances brought the music to a mass audience.
know: His first single paired the blues song That's All Right with Bill Monroe's Blue Moon of Kentucky.
He was drafted into the U.S. Army in 1958 and served in West Germany.
He is the best-selling solo artist of all time by most estimates.

influencedBy.why: He recorded a sped-up version of Bill Monroe's Blue Moon of Kentucky as the B-side of his first single.
He covered Ray Charles's I Got a Woman on his first album.
He had a hit with Carl Perkins's Blue Suede Shoes in 1956.
He covered Tutti Frutti, Long Tall Sally and Rip It Up in 1956.
He recorded Blueberry Hill and called Fats Domino the real king of rock and roll.
He covered several Chuck Berry songs, including Johnny B. Goode and Promised Land.

cousins.why: Both were the defining male idol of their era.
Both became global kings of their genre and its biggest stage presence.

artists.name: Buddy Holly
artists.summary: Buddy Holly wrote, arranged and produced much of his own music in a career of under three years. His Crickets set the two-guitars, bass and drums lineup that rock bands still use.
know: He died in a plane crash on February 3, 1959, later called the day the music died.
The Beatles chose their name partly as a nod to his band, the Crickets.
He opened for Elvis Presley in Lubbock in 1955.

influencedBy.why: Seeing Elvis in Lubbock in 1955 pushed him from country toward rock and roll.
Not Fade Away is built on the Bo Diddley beat, and he recorded Diddley's song Bo Diddley.
He started out playing country songs in Hank Williams's style in the duo Buddy and Bob.
His early Buddy and Bob duo played bluegrass and western material.
He recorded Little Richard's Slippin' and Slidin' and Ready Teddy.
He recorded Chuck Berry's Brown Eyed Handsome Man.

cousins.why: Both wrote a lasting songbook in a few short years before dying young.
Both play bright, simple, catchy songs, and Weezer even wrote a hit called Buddy Holly.

artists.name: Jerry Lee Lewis
artists.summary: Jerry Lee Lewis was rock and roll's wildest piano player, pounding the keys with his hands, feet and elbows. After a 1958 scandal stalled his rock career, he reinvented himself as a country star.
know: He was the last surviving member of Sun Records' Million Dollar Quartet session.
His cousins included country singer Mickey Gilley and preacher Jimmy Swaggart.
His nickname was The Killer.
keyAlbums: Live at the Star Club, Hamburg

influencedBy.why: He idolized Hank Williams and recorded many of his songs.
He named Jimmie Rodgers as an early hero and recorded his songs.
His country boogie piano draws on the Western swing dance bands of Bob Wills's era.

cousins.why: Both are giant voices with hell-raising reputations.
Both are flamboyant piano showmen.

artists.name: Carl Perkins
artists.summary: Carl Perkins was a Sun Records rockabilly pioneer whose Blue Suede Shoes was one of the first records to top pop, country and R&B charts at once. His guitar style was a model for George Harrison and many others.
know: A car crash in 1956 kept him from promoting Blue Suede Shoes on national TV.
The Beatles recorded three of his songs.
He grew up the son of sharecroppers and learned blues from a Black field worker named John Westbrook.
songs: Everybody's Trying to Be My Baby

influencedBy.why: He said Bill Monroe's bluegrass was a major early influence on his playing.
His song Matchbox reworks Blind Lemon Jefferson's Match Box Blues.
Hearing Elvis's first Sun single convinced him to audition for Sam Phillips.

cousins.why: Both play twangy, guitar-driven country-rock built for dancing.
Both blend hillbilly twang with a rockabilly kick.

artists.name: The Everly Brothers
artists.summary: Don and Phil Everly brought Appalachian close-harmony singing into rock and roll. Their two-part harmonies shaped the Beatles, Simon and Garfunkel and the Byrds.
know: Their parents Ike and Margaret Everly were country radio performers.
Bye Bye Love and Wake Up Little Susie were written by Felice and Boudleaux Bryant.
They broke up on stage in 1973 and reunited in 1983.
keyAlbums: A Date with the Everly Brothers
songs: All I Have to Do Is Dream

influencedBy.why: Their sibling harmonies come out of the bluegrass and brother-duet country tradition Bill Monroe helped define.
Their old-time family harmony singing follows the Carter Family tradition.
Don Everly said he borrowed a Bo Diddley-style rhythm for the guitar on Bye Bye Love.
They covered Little Richard's Lucille as a single in 1960.

cousins.why: Both are duos built on tight two-part harmony, and Simon and Garfunkel covered Bye Bye Love.
Both deliver pure, close country harmony singing.

artists.name: Eddie Cochran
artists.summary: Eddie Cochran wrote and played teenage rock anthems with a heavy guitar sound and often overdubbed the parts himself. He died at 21 but his songs became standards for punk and hard rock bands.
know: He died after a taxi crash in England on April 17, 1960.
He performed Twenty Flight Rock in the 1956 film The Girl Can't Help It.
Paul McCartney got into the Quarrymen partly by playing Twenty Flight Rock for John Lennon.

influencedBy.why: He switched from country to rock and roll after Elvis's breakthrough in 1955 and 1956.
He released a cover of Ray Charles's Hallelujah I Love Her So in 1959.
He began in the Cochran Brothers, a country duo playing in the hillbilly style Hank Williams made famous.

cousins.why: Both made short, snarling teenage anthems, and Sid Vicious covered C'mon Everybody.
Both wrote fast, simple songs about teenage frustration.

artists.name: Ray Charles
artists.summary: Ray Charles fused gospel with rhythm and blues in the mid-1950s, creating a template for soul music, and later crossed genre lines with country and jazz records.
know: He had lost his sight by age 7, likely from glaucoma.
Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music (1962) was a No. 1 album.
His 'Georgia on My Mind' became Georgia's official state song in 1979.
keyAlbums: Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music

influencedBy.why: Charles has said he closely imitated Nat King Cole's singing and piano style early in his career.
Jordan's jump blues was a model for Charles's early small-band rhythm and blues.
Charles cited Tatum as the pianist he most admired.
He recorded credited covers of 'Your Cheatin' Heart' and 'Hey, Good Lookin'' and said he grew up loving country radio.

cousins.why: The other 1950s figure who fused Black and white music into a new mainstream sound.
A genre-crossing interpreter who brought country, jazz and pop together.

artists.name: Sam Cooke
artists.summary: Sam Cooke was lead singer of the gospel group the Soul Stirrers before crossing over to pop, and his smooth phrasing and business independence made him one of soul's founders.
know: He founded his own label, SAR Records, and owned his publishing.
'A Change Is Gonna Come' was inspired in part by Bob Dylan's 'Blowin' in the Wind'.
He was shot and killed in Los Angeles in December 1964 at age 33.
keyAlbums: Live at the Harlem Square Club, 1963
songs: Bring It On Home to Me

influencedBy.why: Cooke said hearing 'Blowin' in the Wind' pushed him to write 'A Change Is Gonna Come'.
His smooth pop crossover followed the path Cole had opened for Black singers.

cousins.why: A founder of his genre who wrote his own songs and died young.
A defining voice of his genre whose influence far outlived a short career.

artists.name: James Brown
artists.summary: James Brown led the shift from soul to funk in the late 1960s by putting rhythm first, and his bands' grooves became the most sampled music in hip-hop.
know: He paid for the recording of Live at the Apollo (1963) after King Records doubted it would sell.
Clyde Stubblefield's drum break on 'Funky Drummer' is one of the most sampled in history.
He was among the first inductees into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1986.
songs: Papa's Got a Brand New Bag
Get Up (I Feel Like Being a) Sex Machine
Say It Loud – I'm Black and I'm Proud

influencedBy.why: Brown idolized Little Richard, and his Famous Flames even filled Richard's tour dates when Richard left rock and roll.
Brown named Louis Jordan as his childhood idol and model for a showman bandleader.
Charles's gospel-into-R&B fusion laid the ground for Brown's early soul records.

cousins.why: Built Afrobeat on hypnotic, horn-driven funk grooves led by a commanding bandleader.
Hip-hop's first DJ, who looped funk breaks like Brown's for dancers.

artists.name: Tito Puente
artists.summary: Timbales player and bandleader who led one of the great New York mambo orchestras. He helped carry Afro-Cuban dance music into the American mainstream.
know: He wrote "Oye Como Va," which Santana turned into a rock hit in 1970.
He served in the US Navy in World War II and studied at Juilliard on the GI Bill.
He won five Grammy Awards.

influencedBy.why: Gene Krupa's drumming in Benny Goodman's band is widely cited as what drew the young Puente to the drums.
Gillespie's Afro-Cuban jazz of the late 1940s set the template for the mambo-jazz blend Puente's band played.
Puente's big band arrangements drew on the punchy brass sections of swing orchestras like Basie's.

cousins.why: A drummer who led his band from behind the kit.
A bandleader who made the rhythm section the star.

artists.name: Celia Cruz
artists.summary: Cuban singer known as the Queen of Salsa. Her powerful voice and stage presence made her the face of salsa for five decades.
know: She was lead singer of La Sonora Matancera through the 1950s.
Her trademark shout was "¡Azúcar!"
She left Cuba in 1960 and was never allowed to return.

influencedBy.why: She recorded a string of albums with Puente's orchestra in the 1960s, which shaped her move into New York salsa.

cousins.why: The crowned queen of her genre with a commanding voice.
A singer whose joy and phrasing defined an era of dance music.

artists.name: Antônio Carlos Jobim
artists.summary: Brazilian composer and pianist who wrote most of the bossa nova standards. Songs like "The Girl from Ipanema" made him one of the most recorded songwriters of the 20th century.
know: He co-wrote "The Girl from Ipanema" with lyricist Vinicius de Moraes.
He made a 1967 album with Frank Sinatra.
Rio de Janeiro's main international airport is named after him.

influencedBy.why: Gilberto's guitar rhythm and hushed vocals became the frame for Jobim's songs on the first bossa nova records.
The soft dynamics and extended harmony of 1950s cool jazz fed directly into bossa nova's sound.

cousins.why: A composer whose songs became standards for everyone else.
A songwriter with unusually rich harmony.

artists.name: João Gilberto

keyAlbums: O Amor, o Sorriso e a Flor

cousins.why: Hushed voice and intricate guitar.
Soft, intimate singing that draws the listener in.

artists.name: Ravi Shankar
artists.summary: Sitar master who brought Indian classical music to Western audiences. He shaped 1960s rock and jazz through his work with George Harrison and others.

He taught sitar to George Harrison and played the Monterey Pop and Woodstock festivals.
He was the father of Norah Jones and Anoushka Shankar.

cousins.why: A spiritual seeker who stretched improvisation over drones and modes.
Meditative, devotional music built on long improvisation.

artists.name: Buddy Guy
artists.summary: A wild, explosive guitarist whose stinging tone and showmanship bridged Chicago blues and rock. Clapton, Hendrix and Stevie Ray Vaughan all named him a favorite.

Picked up T-Bone's flashy electric showmanship.

cousins.why: Loud, feedback-friendly guitar played with theatrical abandon.
Explosive, unpredictable stage showman.

artists.name: Albert King

He was backed by Booker T. and the MGs on his Stax recordings.

influencedBy.why: Named T-Bone among the electric players he learned from.

cousins.why: Stax house sound with lean, punchy grooves.
Stax-era Memphis star with raw emotional delivery.

artists.name: Freddie King
artists.summary: A Texas-born guitarist who mixed Texas and Chicago styles into punchy instrumentals and big-voiced blues. He was a major influence on the British blues boom.

Eric Clapton recorded several songs associated with him, including Have You Ever Loved a Woman.

influencedBy.why: Moved to Chicago as a teen and studied Muddy's band in the clubs.
Took the Texas electric single-note approach T-Bone pioneered.

cousins.why: Guitar-hero blues rock built on the same bends and tone.
Long, driving guitar jams rooted in blues.

artists.name: Nina Simone
artists.summary: A classically trained pianist and singer who blended jazz, gospel, blues and classical and became a fierce voice of the civil rights movement.
know: She trained to be a concert pianist and studied at Juilliard.
She wrote Mississippi Goddam in response to the 1963 killing of Medgar Evers and the Birmingham church bombing.
Her version of I Loves You, Porgy was her first hit in 1959.

cousins.why: A singer and writer who openly reveres Simone and shares her mix of art and activism.
A gospel-rooted pianist-singer who became a civil rights era voice.

artists.name: Herbie Hancock
artists.summary: A pianist who was a pillar of Miles Davis's 1960s quintet and later led jazz into funk, electronics and hip-hop.

Head Hunters became one of the best selling jazz albums of its time.
Rockit, with its scratching, was an early MTV hit that brought turntablism to a wide audience.

cousins.why: A keyboard innovator who brought synthesizers into soul and funk.
An electro pioneer working the same machine-funk territory as Rockit.

artists.name: Pharoah Sanders
artists.summary: A tenor saxophonist who carried Coltrane's spiritual quest forward with ecstatic, overblown tones and long meditative grooves.

He played in John Coltrane's final groups in the mid 1960s.
His last album, Promises, was a 2021 collaboration with electronic artist Floating Points.

influencedBy.why: Joined Coltrane's band in 1965 and carried on his spiritual direction afterward.
Played with Sun Ra's Arkestra in New York in the early 1960s.

cousins.why: A musician whose long devotional drones aim at spiritual transcendence.
A producer who carries spiritual jazz into electronic music.

artists.name: Wes Montgomery
artists.summary: A guitarist whose warm thumb-picked tone and octave lines made him the most influential jazz guitarist after Charlie Christian.
know: He played with his thumb instead of a pick, giving him a soft round tone.
He taught himself by learning Charlie Christian solos by ear.
His later pop-leaning albums like A Day in the Life sold very well.

influencedBy.why: Learned guitar by copying Christian's recorded solos note for note.

cousins.why: A guitarist with an instantly recognizable, vocal tone in his genre.
A guitarist who admired Montgomery and reshaped how his instrument sounds.

artists.name: Buck Owens
artists.summary: Leader of the Buckaroos and the main star of the Bakersfield sound, a twangy, electric answer to polished Nashville. He scored a long run of number-one country hits in the 1960s.

He co-hosted the TV show Hee Haw starting in 1969.
His 1988 duet with Dwight Yoakam, "Streets of Bakersfield", went to number one.

I've Got a Tiger by the Tail

He recorded Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and had a hit with it in 1969.

cousins.why: A lean, twangy band built on short, catchy hits.
A tight house-band sound that defined a regional style.

artists.name: Merle Haggard
artists.summary: Singer-songwriter who turned his rough youth and prison time into some of country's most direct songs about working people. With Buck Owens he defined the Bakersfield sound.

Governor Ronald Reagan granted him a full pardon in 1972.
His backing band was called the Strangers.
keyAlbums: A Tribute to the Best Damn Fiddle Player in the World

He recorded a double album tribute to Rodgers, Same Train, a Different Time.
He learned fiddle to honor Wills and recorded a tribute album with former Texas Playboys.
He said seeing Cash's 1958 San Quentin show inspired him to pursue music.
Williams' plainspoken songwriting is a clear model for Haggard's own.

cousins.why: Writes about working-class life from the inside.
A plainspoken songwriter about ordinary working people.

artists.name: George Jones
artists.summary: Widely considered the greatest voice in country music, known for bending notes to wring out every bit of heartbreak. His career ran from 1950s honky-tonk to 1980s classics.
know: His nickname was "the Possum."
He was married to Tammy Wynette from 1969 to 1975 and they recorded many duets.
"He Stopped Loving Her Today" (1980) is often named the greatest country song ever.

influencedBy.why: Williams was his idol, and he recorded the tribute album George Jones Salutes Hank Williams in 1960.
His bending, stretched vocal phrasing draws on Frizzell's style.

cousins.why: A singer who pours raw ache into every line.
A singer other singers point to as the best interpreter of a song.

artists.name: Loretta Lynn
artists.summary: Coal miner's daughter who wrote frank songs about women's real lives: marriage, cheating husbands and birth control. She became one of country's most important songwriters.
know: Several of her songs, including "The Pill", were banned by some radio stations.
Her mentor and close friend was Patsy Cline.
Her 2004 album Van Lear Rose, produced by Jack White, won a Grammy.
keyAlbums: Don't Come Home A-Drinkin' (With Lovin' on Your Mind)
songs: Don't Come Home A-Drinkin' (With Lovin' on Your Mind)

influencedBy.why: Cline mentored her early in Nashville, and Lynn recorded the tribute album I Remember Patsy in 1977.

cousins.why: Sang bluntly about respect and women's lives.
A woman songwriter writing from her own experience.

artists.name: Dolly Parton
artists.summary: Singer, songwriter and entertainer who rose from the Smoky Mountains to global stardom. She wrote classics like "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You" and became a pop culture icon.
know: She has said she wrote "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You" on the same day.
She started on The Porter Wagoner Show in 1967.
Her Imagination Library gives free books to children around the world.

influencedBy.why: She had a hit in 1970 with his "Mule Skinner Blues."

cousins.why: A huge voice that became a pop phenomenon, and she made Dolly's song a global hit.
An entertainer who built an empire on her own terms.

artists.name: Gram Parsons
artists.summary: Pioneer of country rock who pulled the Byrds toward country and formed the Flying Burrito Brothers. He died at 26, but his blend of rock and classic country shaped Americana.
know: He joined the Byrds in 1968 and steered them to make Sweetheart of the Rodeo.
He introduced Emmylou Harris to a wide audience as his duet partner.
He died in 1973 near Joshua Tree, and friends stole his body to cremate it in the desert.

influencedBy.why: Seeing Elvis perform in Waycross, Georgia in 1956 sparked his interest in music.
He was a Haggard devotee and brought "Life in Prison" to the Byrds' Sweetheart of the Rodeo.

The Burritos' twangy electric sound draws on the Bakersfield style of Owens.

cousins.why: A cult act that sold little but shaped later generations.
Influence far bigger than its sales.
A gifted artist who died young with a small, revered catalog.

artists.name: Joan Baez
artists.summary: Soprano who became the leading voice of the early 1960s folk revival and a lifelong activist. She helped introduce Bob Dylan to a wide audience.
know: Her breakthrough came at the 1959 Newport Folk Festival.
She brought a young Bob Dylan on stage during her tours.
She sang at both the 1963 March on Washington and Woodstock.

influencedBy.why: Baez has named Odetta as a key early influence.
Seeger's mix of traditional song and activism was the model for her career.
She recorded a double album of his songs, Any Day Now.
She had a hit covering their "The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down."

cousins.why: A singer whose music was bound up with civil rights.
A pure voice that became a symbol of a movement.

artists.name: Bob Dylan
artists.summary: The most influential songwriter of the rock era, who brought literary lyrics into popular music. He moved from protest folk to electric rock and kept reinventing himself for six decades.
know: He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016.
He went electric at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival, angering many folk fans.
He visited the ailing Woody Guthrie in a New Jersey hospital in 1961.

influencedBy.why: Guthrie was his first great hero; he wrote "Song to Woody" and visited him in hospital.

His high school yearbook said his ambition was to join Little Richard.
In his Nobel lecture he described seeing Holly in Duluth days before Holly died.
He said hearing an Odetta record was the first thing that turned him on to folk singing.

He said the Beatles' chords were outrageous and that they pointed to where music had to go.

cousins.why: A Pulitzer-winning writer who treats lyrics as literature.
A poet who brought literary ambition to rock.

artists.name: Simon & Garfunkel
artists.summary: Duo of songwriter Paul Simon and singer Art Garfunkel whose close harmonies and literate songs made them the best-selling folk rock act of the 1960s.
know: They first recorded as Tom & Jerry in 1957.
Producer Tom Wilson added electric instruments to "The Sound of Silence" without telling them, and it went to number one.

influencedBy.why: They modeled their harmonies on the Everlys and covered "Bye Bye Love" on Bridge over Troubled Water.
Their debut album included a cover of "The Times They Are a-Changin'."
Paul Simon has said early rock and roll like Elvis drew him to music.

cousins.why: Built on tight vocal harmonies and carefully crafted songs.
A harmony group with a songwriter's ear.

artists.name: Joni Mitchell
artists.summary: Canadian singer-songwriter known for confessional lyrics, unusual open guitar tunings and a later move into jazz. Blue is often called one of the greatest albums ever made.

cousins.why: A singular woman artist who writes, arranges and follows her own path.
An experimental songwriter who never stayed in one genre.

artists.name: Leonard Cohen

influencedBy.why: He admired Williams and wrote him into "Tower of Song."

cousins.why: Low baritone vocals and literate, melancholy songs.
Slow, dark songs about love and longing.

artists.name: Nick Drake
artists.summary: English singer-songwriter whose quiet, intricate guitar songs sold poorly in his lifetime but became hugely influential after his death.

cousins.why: A gifted voice with a small catalog who died young.

California soft rock built on multiple songwriters and harmonies.

artists.name: Cream

artists.name: Pink Floyd
